standard.title: Experiment with figurative language
standard.description: Create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings from texts students have experienced
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create and edit literary texts by developing storylines, characters and settings (AC9E4LE05). They have not yet experimented with figurative language — simile, metaphor, personification — as a deliberate craft tool, or used model texts as a source for experimental creative choices.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create and edit literary texts that deliberately experiment with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings drawn from or inspired by texts they have experienced, demonstrating intentional craft choices in their writing.

nodes.label: Reading as a writer: noticing craft choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific craft choices in model texts — figurative language, character techniques, setting construction — and explain how those choices create effects they can learn from.
nodes.minimum_width: In a model literary text, identify at least two craft choices the author has made (figurative language, character detail, setting description) and explain what effect each creates and what can be learned from it.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a range of model texts for craft choices, building a repertoire of specific techniques — types of figurative language used, how characters are introduced and developed, how settings are constructed — that can be drawn on in their own writing. Create a visual or written map of craft choices from texts experienced.
wider: Analyse how First Nations Australian authors and illustrators make craft choices — examining how figurative language, character description and setting construction reflect cultural ways of knowing and representing the world
Compare craft choices across literary texts in different forms (picture book, poem, short story) and discuss how the form shapes which craft choices are available
success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific craft choices in a model text and explains the effect each creates.
Connects the craft choice to something that can be applied in their own writing — not just appreciates it.

nodes.label: Experimenting with figurative language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can deliberately experiment with figurative language — simile, metaphor, personification — in their literary writing, making choices about which type of imagery to use and where to use it.
nodes.minimum_width: In a draft literary text, include at least two examples of deliberately chosen figurative language (at least two different types) and explain the effect intended with each choice.
nodes.typical_width: Draft a literary text that demonstrates deliberate use of figurative language — simile, metaphor and/or personification — at key points. Explain the craft choices made: why this image here, what comparison is intended, what effect is sought. Draw on imagery from model texts as inspiration or starting points.
wider: Experiment with the same scene or description using different types of figurative language and compare the effects — developing a feel for when simile vs. metaphor vs. personification serves the moment better
Experiment with extended metaphor across a short piece, developing a central comparison and sustaining it throughout
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to draw on figurative language experimentation as source material for extended narrative creation, and Node 4 requires them to edit figurative language for effect. Students who have not yet made deliberate figurative language choices cannot meaningfully attempt either — their drafts will lack the intentional imagery that editing and narrative integration depends on.

response_modes.reason: Students often produce figurative language that is generic ('the sun was like a ball') rather than purposeful. Encountering a range of model images — including unexpected comparisons, culturally specific imagery, and imagery from texts that have been studied — helps students develop a broader sense of what is possible and what makes an image work.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Experimenting with figurative language across genres, forms, and inspirational sources — including imagery from First Nations Australian authors — is genuinely rich creative territory. Advancing students can develop an authorial sense of imagery as a deliberate tool, comparing the effects of different choices and building a personal creative vocabulary.
success_criteria: Includes at least two examples of figurative language (using different types) in their literary text.
Can explain the intended effect of each figurative language choice — the choice is deliberate, not accidental.

nodes.label: Experimenting with storylines, characters and settings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw on storylines, characters and settings from texts they have experienced as source material for their own literary writing, making deliberate choices about what to adapt, extend, or transform.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a literary text that draws on at least one element — storyline, character, or setting — from a text they have experienced, explaining what they borrowed and how they transformed or extended it.
nodes.typical_width: Create a literary text that uses model texts as creative source material — adapting storylines, borrowing character types, transforming settings — and explain the creative choices made. Demonstrate awareness of what was taken from models and how it has been made their own.
wider: Experiment with retelling a story from a different point of view or in a different setting, discussing how the change transforms the narrative and what the experiment reveals about the original
Create a literary text inspired by texts from culturally different contexts — adapting story structures, characters or settings from those texts and reflecting on what the adaptation requires

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together craft reading (node 1), figurative language experimentation (node 2), and narrative construction into a literary text that demonstrates authorial intentionality — the full demand of the descriptor's 'experimenting with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings' clause.

success_criteria: Creates a literary text that incorporates at least one element drawn from a model text and demonstrates how it has been transformed.
Can explain the creative choices made — what was borrowed, what was changed, and why.

nodes.label: Editing for effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can review and edit their literary writing to improve figurative language, narrative development, and characterisation, making changes with reference to intended effect.
nodes.minimum_width: Review a draft and identify at least two specific changes that would improve the text's use of figurative language or narrative elements, and make those changes with an explanation of the intended improvement.
nodes.typical_width: Edit a literary text using negotiated criteria, focusing on precision of figurative language choices, character development, and setting construction. Reflect on how the editing process has changed the text and what the changes have achieved.
wider: Exchange drafts with a peer and provide specific feedback on figurative language and narrative choices — practising the language of craft critique as well as authorship
Compare an early draft with a final version and trace how the editing choices have improved specific effects — developing metacognitive awareness of the revision process

response_modes.reason: Editing for effect requires students to reason from intended effect backwards to the text — 'I want the reader to feel X here, so I need to change Y in my figurative language'. This purposeful editing orientation needs to be made explicit; students without the scaffold tend to fix surface errors rather than craft choices.

success_criteria: Makes at least two deliberate editing changes to figurative language or narrative elements and explains the effect intended by each change.
Can identify the difference between surface-level editing (spelling, grammar) and craft-level editing (figurative language, characterisation) and demonstrates both.
